'''''Cerastium fontanum''''', also called '''mouse-ear chickweed''', '''common mouse-ear''', or '''starweed''', is a species of mat-forming [[perennial plant|perennial]] or, rarely, [[annual plant]]. It is native to Europe but [[introduced species|introduced]] elsewhere. Its identifying characteristics are tear-shaped leaves growing opposite one another in a star pattern, [[Trichome|hairy]] leaves, and small white flowers. Mouse-ear chickweed typically grows to 4"-8" tall and spreads horizontally along the ground via the formation of roots wherever the stem falls over and contacts the ground.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242000274 |title=Cerastium fontanum in Flora of North America @ |publisher=Efloras.org |date= |accessdate=2022-05-01}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/ClassificationServlet?source=display&classid=CEFO2|title=USDA Plants Database}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Mouse-ear Chickweed (49195024206).jpg|left|thumb]]
''Cerastium fontanum'' is a low growing plant covered with small hairs which are not sticky, that is, without glandular tips. The erect flowering stems up to {{convert|45|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and leaves, opposite, up to {{convert|20|mm|in|abbr=on}} long without stalks. It has prostrate branches which do not bear flowers. The 5 petals are shorter than the sepals or a little longer and are deeply divided. The flowers have 10 [[stamen]]s with 5 separate [[Stigma (botany)|styles]].<ref name="CTW-68">Clapham, A.R., Tutin, T.G. and Warburg, E.F. 1968. ''Excursion Flora of the British Isles''. Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-04656-4}}</ref><ref>Parnell, J and Curtis, T. 2012. ''Webb's An Irish Flora.'' Cork University Press {{ISBN|978-185918-4783}}</ref>

==Habitat==
It is common in grassland and along roadsides.<ref name="CTW-68"/>

==Distribution==
It is native to Europe, Greenland, the Himalayas and Japan.<ref name="POWO">{{cite web |work=Plants of the World Online |title=''Cerastium fontanum'' Baumg. |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden, Kew |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:152255-1 |access-date=16 April 2023 }}</ref>  It is common throughout [[Great Britain]]<ref name="CTW-68"/> and [[Ireland]].<ref>Scannell and Synnott, D. 1972. ''Census Catalogue of the Flora of Ireland.''  Dublin</ref> It has been introduced to the Falkland Islands and MacQuarie Island,<ref name="POWO"/> and to many other places around the world, including all 50 of the [[United States]] and all provinces and territories of [[Canada]] except [[Nunavut]]. <ref>{{cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/ClassificationServlet?source=display&classid=CEFO2|title=USDA Plants Database}}</ref>

==Etymology==
''Cerastium'' is derived from the [[Greek language|Greek]] word for 'horned',{{source needed|reason= Gledhill writes: 'Cerastium Horned, κερας (the fruiting capsule’s shape)'. Gledhill explanation is ambiguous as he does not mention any word that means 'horned'. Κερας is 'horn', not 'horned'. Κεράστης actually means 'horned', but a more reliable and consistent source than Gledhill is needed in this instance.|date=April 2025}} in reference to the shape of its fruit capsule.<ref name="Gledhill-2008">Gledhill, David (2008). "The Names of Plants". Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback).  pp 99, 169</ref>

''Fontanum'' means 'of fountains', 'of springs', or 'of fast-running streams'. It is a cognate with 'fountain' and 'font'.<ref name="Gledhill-2008" />
